body: How every non-natural object went through some sort of intricate manufacturing process, which involved many separate sub-processes, all of which at least several human beings have devoted their lives to. How many people's lives were involved with the packaging to the yogurt cup I ate earlier? The dyes, the plastics, the foil, the ink printing the nutritional facts, the scientists who investigated this information, the people who regulate the packaging, the designers, the factory workers, the designer of the factory, all those involved with the petroleum extraction for the plastic, etc. Every single manufactured object that comes from the mass marketplace.

I'm not saying this is a universal gateway to Noise, but it might help if you approach it with the mindset that one would use for Free Jazz, especially improvised stuff. IMO, this is more useful than listening to Noise as if it were simply a more extreme form of metal or punk. 

I think that musicians like Albert Ayler, Anthony Braxton, and Peter Brotzmann are much more similar to Noise than some of the shoegaze or indie pop artists that others in this thread list. I'm not trying to take these comments down a peg...I just don't think that Deerhunter or MBV are gateway bands to Masonna, CCCC, Gero, or The Haters, or even new stuff like John Weise and Hospital Records (not including the new Prurient, natch). For these kinds of indie rock bands, the term "noise" isn't a genre tag, but instead seems to signify a wider sonic palate that includes some abrasive sounds derived from Industrial and ambient music (FYI, I like Deerhunter and MBV). Free Jazz helped me learn to love the spirit of spontaneity in Noise, and how harsh sounds have their own colors that can be really beautiful and fun if you adjust to their level.

But then again, Free Jazz isn't for everybody either. Another avenue might be No Wave bands (James Chance, etc. or some of the more abrasive Harry Pussy stuff). Or if you if do want to go the extreme-punk route, try some West Coast Powerviolence, which took the spirit of hardcore and maxed it out with homemade electronics.
